description: Solo full-stack developer building a status-page-style tool for lunar south pole landing sites. The idea: treat each site like a monitored service is the Sun up (power)? Is Earth in view (comms link)? Slip the launch date and watch which sites survive the delay. Built on JPL Horizons data, with calendar exports and an API so the results plug into existing planning workflows. Background in cybersecurity and infrastructure monitoring at the City of Oshawa
summary: Moon Status is a status page for the Moon. Pick any landing site and time, and it tells you in plain words whether a lander there would have sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for radio, and when that changes over the next 30 days. That is the question the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge asks, and it decides whether a mission survives: near the south pole the Sun barely clears the horizon, and in 2025 the IM-2 lander came down about 370 m from its target and lost the mission a day later. Moon Status covers 21 real sites or any typed coordinates, compares two plans, and uses NASA’s LOLA terrain at three south-pole sites to show how far a landing can miss and still work. Every number comes from NASA JPL Horizons, checked against Apollo 11’s landing (10.7° against NASA’s 10.8°), and the same answers are open through an API and an AI assistant connector.
details:
What it does
Moon Status is a status page for the Moon. Pick a landing site and a time, and it tells you whether a lander there would have sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for radio. It covers 21 real landing sites, from Apollo 11 to the south pole, or any coordinates you type in, for any hour from 1960 to 2100.

Why it matters
Near the south pole the Sun barely clears the horizon and Earth sits low. A few hundred metres or a few days can decide whether a lander survives. In March 2025 the IM-2 lander came down about 370 m from its target, on its side in a crater, and the mission ended the next day. Agencies plan for this with specialist software. Students, reporters and smaller teams have nothing quick to check.

How it works

  • Console: status for every site, the next change (sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, Earth set) and a 30-day timeline of power and link.
  • Compare: two plans side by side, with a plain-language report on what changed.
  • Miss: real NASA terrain around three south-pole sites. Click the map or type coordinates to see how often a landing still works for landers that land within 100, 250 or 320 m of their aim.
  • Watch: calendar reminders, or an email when a plan stops working.
  • API and AI connector: the same answers as JSON, CSV and calendar files, plus a connector an AI assistant can query.

Benefits and impact
It turns a specialist calculation into a one-line answer anyone can read: “No power: the Sun is 1.7° up, under the 2° shadow allowance.” Mission planners can test a slipped date in seconds. Teachers can show why the south pole is hard. Developers and AI assistants can build on the open API.

How I know it’s right
Every Sun and Earth position comes from NASA JPL Horizons. For Apollo 11’s landing the app gives a Sun height of 10.7°, and NASA published 10.8°. The terrain directions match the elevation map’s own projection to within 0.004°. Where the 80 m map is too coarse, as with the crater that ended IM-2, the app says so instead of guessing.

Tools
TypeScript, React, Node.js and PostgreSQL for the app; Python with rasterio, NumPy and pyproj for terrain; hosted on my own home server behind Cloudflare. Source code: https://github.com/dan-od/lunar-landing

What’s creative
The status-page idea itself: instead of charts, you get an answer and a reason. The Miss map shows not just whether a target works, but how much room for error a landing has.

What I considered
NASA’s fair-use rules (one request at a time, every answer saved), accessibility (keyboard, screen readers, colour-blind safe symbols), phones, and never inventing data: sites without terrain or citable coordinates are left out with the reason shown.

What’s next
A background worker that prepares terrain for any new site automatically, and NASA’s other elevation maps to extend Miss beyond the south pole.
